entries.title: Islamic Golden Age of Science
entries.summary: The Islamic Golden Age refers to a long period when scholars in Muslim societies made major advances in medicine, mathematics, astronomy, optics, chemistry, and philosophy, often building on Greek, Persian, and Indian knowledge.
entries.detailed_information: Centers such as Baghdad, Cordoba, Cairo, and later Samarkand supported hospitals, observatories, libraries, and scholarly networks. The translation movement into Arabic preserved and transformed earlier sciences. Algebra, experimental optics, medical encyclopedias, and refined astronomy are among notable contributions. The phrase 'Golden Age' is a modern historical label; flourishing was uneven across time and region.
entries.location: Across Islamic lands — Iraq, Persia, Egypt, al-Andalus, Central Asia
entries.historical_significance: Shaped global scientific history and later European learning via transmission.
entries.disputed_notes: Chronological boundaries of a single 'Golden Age' are debated by historians.
related_questions: What was the House of Wisdom?
entries.source: George Saliba, Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance

entries.title: Al-Khwarizmi and Algebra
entries.summary: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi was a 9th-century scholar whose works on algebra and arithmetic deeply influenced mathematics; the word 'algorithm' derives from his name.
entries.detailed_information: Working in the Abbasid intellectual milieu, al-Khwarizmi wrote Kitab al-Jabr wa al-Muqabala, a foundational algebra text. His arithmetic helped transmit decimal positional methods. Latin translations later shaped European mathematics.
entries.historical_significance: Cornerstone figure in the history of algebra and computational methods.
related_questions: What was the House of Wisdom?
entries.source: George Saliba, Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance

entries.title: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) and Medicine
entries.summary: Ibn Sina was a Persian polymath whose Canon of Medicine became a standard medical reference in Islamic and European learned traditions for centuries.
entries.detailed_information: Ibn Sina contributed to medicine, philosophy, and natural science. The Qanun fi al-Tibb organized medical knowledge systematically. He also wrote extensively on metaphysics and logic. His influence extended through Latin 'Avicenna' translations.
entries.historical_significance: One of the most influential physicians-philosophers in world history.

sources.author: Classical biobibliographical tradition
